newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stripped of key defense in Medicaid case.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stripped of key defense in Medicaid case.

text.p: In a key ruling two days before the start of trial, a Florida judge said Wednesday that tobacco companies cannot use public knowledge of the dangers of cigarette smoking as a defense.

Lawyers for both sides said the ruling, issued by Palm Beach Circuit Judge Harold Cohen, would have a significant impact on the tobacco industry's ability to defend itself against Florida's billion-dollar lawsuit, which seeks to recover the Medicaid costs of treating smoking-related illnesses.
"It means they have no defenses," said W. C. Gentry, a lawyer representing the state.
"By this ruling the only thing they can try to prove is that cigarettes don't cause disease, the product wasn't defective, that they couldn't make a safer cigarette," he said.
Jury selection in the widely watched lawsuit was scheduled to begin Friday, with testimony expected to start in early September.

The tobacco companies, arguing what evidence can be presented to the jury ultimately selected to hear the case, wanted to claim that the only way the state should be able to recover damages was if it can prove that Medicaid recipients were deceived as to the dangers of smoking.
"If not, there can be no injury," Philip Morris Cos. Inc. attorney Peter Bleakley said.
He said Cohen's ruling "seriously impairs our ability to defend ourselves, here or elsewhere."
"The ruling is wrong," he said. "The plaintiffs should have the burden of proving what we did caused injury."
Bleakley said the ruling could be grounds for reversible error should the case go to an appeals court.
The ruling came on a motion made by the state to bar use of depositions taken from 25 Medicaid recipients who were interviewed about their Medicaid-related injuries.
Cohen himself called the ruling one of the most important he had made in the case.
